Another useful capability of brazing is the so-called ‘step-brazing’ process, where sub-assemblies are joined using a braze alloy of melting temperature T . Critical mating surfaces of the sub-assembly are then machined 1 then brazed to other sub-assemblies using a braze alloy with melting temperature T . Because the melting 2 temperature of braze alloy used in step 2 is less than the alloy used in step one, the prior joints remain untouched. As an example, a waveguide input coupler is brazed at T along with the primary cell stack. The 1 mating feature between the waveguide coupler and cover plate is machined to a precise dimension so that it mates to the cell stack. The cell stack is then brazed the waveguide feed in Step 2. From an RF perspective, a key feature of split-cell structures is that surface currents do not flow across any bonding junctions. While conventional AS are typically composed of individual discs which are turned, split-cell AS are manufactured using only multi-axis milling. Split-cell structures significantly reduce the AS part count and greatly simplify the assembly process, offering potentially significant cost savings. Issues such as longitudinal alignment between parts, as well as straightness of beamline bore, can be significant. Another advantage of split-cell structures is the ability to implement so-called ‘distributed coupling’ [4]. In this topology, internal waveguides run alongside the accelerator cavities, and power is fed to each cell directly. In comparison to conventional side-coupled or aperture coupled AS, the distributed coupling approach enables cavity shapes to be optimized solely for high gradients, maximized shunt impedance and permits more localized power reflection during breakdown events compared to traditionally coupled structures.
